title: Fully funded scholarships for Central Asian students 2027
summary: The real government scholarship programmes for bachelor's and master's study, what each one covers, how to read a fully funded offer, and how to avoid scam pages.

sources.title: Study in Korea: Global Korea Scholarship portal
Erasmus+: Erasmus Mundus Joint Master Degrees

review_note: Verified on the fetched official Türkiye Scholarships page (support categories listed; no figures or dates on the page, so the calendar is referred to without dates). All other citations are official homepages that were not read in depth: the GKS notice pages returned 404, the CSC page returned 412, and the Stipendium Hungaricum site showed a certificate error. Therefore no benefit amounts, quotas or deadlines are stated for GKS, CSC, Stipendium Hungaricum, DAAD or Erasmus Mundus. Erasmus Mundus is described as master's-level, which should be confirmed on its official page.
body:
## In short

- A fully funded scholarship covers a defined set of costs. "Fully funded" in an advertisement can mean very different things, so read the official list of benefits.
- Only apply through official programme websites. Many scam pages copy programme names and ask for fees, bank details or "processing" payments.
- Most government scholarships have strict eligibility rules on nationality, age, previous study and language. Check these before you spend time on an essay.
- The programmes below are real and listed by their official providers. Deadlines and benefit details change each year, so confirm them on the official page before you apply.

## How to read "fully funded"

Ask five questions about any scholarship:

1. Does it cover tuition, or only part of it?
2. Is there a monthly allowance, and is it paid in full each month?
3. Does it include accommodation, health insurance, and a flight or travel allowance?
4. Is there a language year or preparatory course before the degree starts?
5. Who decides, and at which stage: the home country, the host university or the programme?

Write the answers down. If a page does not answer them, the answer is not yet known, so do not assume.

## Türkiye Scholarships

Türkiye Scholarships is run by the Presidency for Turks Abroad and Related Communities (YTB) and is open to international applicants for bachelor's, master's and doctoral study at Turkish universities. The official site lists support categories including a monthly stipend, accommodation, health insurance, a language course, and a flight ticket. The application calendar is published on the official site, and you should check it for the current cycle rather than relying on dates in third-party guides.

Plan for a language stage. Many programmes are taught in Turkish, and a preparatory year may be part of the scholarship. Read the offer letter carefully before you accept a place.

## GKS: Global Korea Scholarship

The Global Korea Scholarship is run by the Korean government through the National Institute for International Education and is announced on the Study in Korea portal, studyinkorea.go.kr. It has undergraduate tracks for students from partner countries. Applications may go through a Korean embassy track or a university track, and the two have different timelines and selection steps.

GKS guidelines are published for each intake year and set out eligibility, age limits, language requirements and the benefits. The guidelines are the authority on those points, so read the notice for the year you are applying for, not an earlier one. Benefits in the past have included tuition, a monthly allowance, airfare and language training. Confirm each benefit in the current notice.

## Chinese Government Scholarship (CSC)

The Chinese Government Scholarship is administered by the China Scholarship Council, which publishes the programme on csc.edu.cn. Scholarship offers are linked to a university place, so you apply both for the scholarship and for admission at a Chinese university. Some university-based offers are run by the university itself. Check which category applies to the programme you want.

Read the CSC guidance for the benefits package, which varies by level and by category. Do not rely on a summary that lists fixed amounts from a previous year.

## Stipendium Hungaricum

Stipendium Hungaricum is the Hungarian government scholarship programme for international students, administered through the official programme website. It covers places at Hungarian higher education institutions, and benefits are set by the programme rules for each intake. Many students compare it with self-financed places at Hungarian universities, so check both routes.

## DAAD

The German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD) runs a large scholarship database. Much of its funding is aimed at master's study, doctoral research and professional training rather than first degrees. Use the database filters to check whether anything fits a bachelor's application, and read the eligibility section carefully, because some funding requires prior study, work experience or a specific subject area.

## Erasmus Mundus

Erasmus Mundus Joint Master Degrees are European master's programmes run by consortia of universities with EU funding. They are for master's study, not bachelor's study. If you are planning a bachelor's degree, treat Erasmus Mundus as a later option, and check the current call on the official Erasmus+ site.

## How to avoid scams

- Apply only through the official programme website or a link on it.
- Never pay an application or "processing" fee to a scholarship programme that is free to apply for.
- Do not send your passport scan or bank details to anyone who contacts you by messaging app and says they are an official.
- Check the programme name, the country and the deadline against the official site.
- Be cautious of pages that show "2027 open" with no official source.

## Building a shortlist

Choose five to eight programmes that match your nationality, subject and level. Note the deadline and the number of documents for each. Start the one with the earliest deadline first. Most scholarships need a reference letter, a school transcript, a language certificate and a motivation statement, and some require a medical form. Prepare a master set of documents so that each application takes less time to finish.

## Application stories and what reviewers look for

Scholarship committees read many applications, and they look for clear evidence rather than general enthusiasm. A good application explains why this programme, why this university and why you, with examples from school, community work or a job. Avoid long lists of awards without context. Name one or two projects, explain your role, and say what you learned.

Motivation letters should be specific to the programme. Mention a course, a research area or a faculty member you have read about, and explain how it fits your plans for work in Central Asia or elsewhere. Keep the letter within the length the programme sets, and have a teacher check the grammar and facts.

## Documents to prepare once

Most scholarship forms ask for the same core set: passport, school transcripts, graduation certificate, language certificate, a passport photo, a medical form in some cases, and two references. Prepare these once and store scanned copies in a folder with clear names. Where a document must be translated or legalised, start that early, because official offices can take weeks.

Reference letters work best when the referee knows your work well. Give them your draft motivation letter, the programme name and the deadline, and a short list of achievements they can mention. Ask at least three weeks before the deadline.

## Interviews and selection

Some scholarships include an interview, sometimes online, held by the embassy, the university or the programme office. Prepare short answers about your motivation, your study plan and your country's needs. Practise with a friend in English, and if the interview is in another language, practise in that language too. Dress and speak clearly, and have your application documents on hand.

## What to do if you are not selected

Many strong applicants are not selected in their first attempt. Ask the programme whether feedback is available. Keep your application documents, and apply to a second scholarship or a self-financed place at the same time. A conditional admission at a university can also keep your options open while you improve your application for the next cycle.

## Checklist

- [ ] Confirm nationality and age eligibility on the official programme page.
- [ ] Read the benefits list and write down exactly what is covered.
- [ ] Check the application calendar for the current cycle.
- [ ] Confirm whether a language year or preparatory course is included.
- [ ] Prepare transcripts, certificates and language results before the deadline.
- [ ] Apply through official channels only, and never pay a fee to apply.
- [ ] Keep a backup university offer in case the scholarship is not awarded.
